newsitem.title: JAPAN: SPEED SKATING-CHAREST SETS WORLD MARK, SECOND IN FINAL.
newsitem.headline: SPEED SKATING-CHAREST SETS WORLD MARK, SECOND IN FINAL.

text.p: Canada's Isabelle Charest set a world record in the 500 metres heats at the world short track speed skating championships on Saturday but a three-woman crash left her as runner-up in the final.
The only competitor left standing, Yang Yang of China, who had been trailing, skated to victory in 45.946 seconds.
The win left Yang tied for first with South Korea's Chun Lee-kyung for the overall lead. Charest and Chun's team mate Won Hye-kyung are tied for third.
Derrick Campbell of Canada took the men's 500 metres in 43.424 seconds, edging South Korean Kim Dong-sung and Satoru Terao of Japan.
Canadian Marc Gagnon, who placed fourth, holds a one-point lead over Campbell in the race for the men's overall title.

Charest became the first woman to dip below 45 seconds in the 500 metres when she blazed to a 44.867-second heat victory, the first world record set in the White Ring venue which will host short track events at next year's Nagano Olympics.
The Canadian skater, who followed that with a 44.971 seconds semifinal win, had just grabbed the lead from Wang Chunlu of China on the last curve of the four-woman final when the crash happened.
"It happened very fast," said Charest. "I felt the Chinese on the outside. Our blades clicked and we went down. Maybe we were too close to one another."
Third-placed Marinella Canclini of Italy was also taken out.
"It's kind of scary when you fall three at a time," said Charest. "My suit was ripped and I was afraid of getting cut."

Yang crossed the finish line alone as her competitors were getting to their feet. Charest finished 6.104 seconds behind, followed by Canclini, another 2.324 seconds back. Wang was disqualified for cross-tracking.
"I was quite surprised when I saw the crash," said Yang. "I felt sorry for those strong athletes who fell. On the other hand, it was good luck for me."
Charest said she was satisfied to twice fulfill her goal of skating under 45 seconds, "although I would have preferred to finish (the final) standing".
She discounted suggestions that the Chinese may have engineered the crash as a tactical move.
"I don't think the Chinese team would team-skate," she said. "I know they are racing individually. Crashing is part of the sport and we accept it."
Although skaters who are impeded in earlier rounds are automatically advanced, the sport has no automatic provisions to rectify interference in finals.

"The referee does have the possibility to re-run the final," said John Hall, the International Skating Union's short track technical committee chairman. "But sometimes it's felt to be unfair to the other skaters. So for now, the anomaly exists."

Yang lowered the world mark set by Charest at last year's championships to 45.18 seconds last November in Beijing. Charest also recorded an unratified record of 45.11 seconds earlier this month in Calgary.
In the men's 500 metres, the lead shifted several times before Campbell regained it on the final lap.
"It was kind of a crazy race," said Campbell, a former hockey player and figure skater. "So much happened. I had my work cut out for me. I was first on the first lap, then suddnnly I was fourth."
